Taught art in Atlanta public schools for approximately fifty years.
Saved money from her Social Security payments for her grandchildren’s education. Helped her grandson, filmmaker Shelton Jackson “Spike” Lee, attend Morehouse College and New York University.
Provided early funding for Lee’s first feature film, She’s Gotta Have It.
Married postal employee Richard Jackson Shelton, who died in 1976.
Spelman College records also identify her as Zimmie Retha Shelton.

Taught mathematics at Jack Yates High School in Houston before settling in Atlanta with her husband, Edward Lloyd Simon.
Worked in painting, sculpture and printmaking, alongside interests in music and poetry.
Helped found the National Conference of Negro Artists and participated in Atlanta’s civic arts leadership.
Also appears in biographical sources as Jewel Alma Woodard Simon.

Earned her undergraduate degree, summa cum laude, from Atlanta University.
Studied painting with Hale Woodruff and sculpture with Alice Dunbar.
Became the first Black graduate awarded a bachelor of fine arts degree by the Atlanta School of Art in 1967.
Her Atlanta University degree is dated 1930 by the Texas State Historical Association and 1931 by the biographical directory reproduced by Prabook.

Grew up on Auburn Avenue as the daughter of Wesley Chapel Redding and Ellen Redding.
Preserved local history through oral histories and her work as historian of First Congregational Church.
Served on the Auburn Avenue Research Library’s board and became known for her knowledge of Atlanta’s Black community.
Her death year differs between sources: Atlanta History Center’s authority record gives 1993, while Henderson’s South-View book lists 2003.

Attended Morris Brown College and Turner Theological Seminary.
Helped organize the 1960 campaign against segregation at Rich’s department store while a Morris Brown student.

Was eighteen when a white mob killed him on the Crogman School playground in Atlanta on June 15, 1930.
Was the son of minister Gaddus Johnson Hubert and educator Pearl Parks Hubert, and a nephew of Morehouse leader Charles Dubois Hubert.
His family faced further attacks after his killing.
Morehouse’s 2025 commencement records identify him as Dennis O. Hubert.

Attended Morehouse College and Atlanta University.
Sources differ on his Morehouse attendance dates: a family account places it in 1922–1923, while the New Georgia Encyclopedia gives 1924.

Led Ebenezer Baptist Church’s choir and served for decades as organist and music director.
Raised her family with Martin Luther King Sr. and was the mother of Martin Luther King Jr.
Was the daughter of Ebenezer pastor Adam Daniel Williams and Jennie Celeste Williams.
Was killed while playing the church organ during Sunday worship in June 1974.
Sources differ on her birth year: the Stanford King Institute gives 1903, while Atlanta History Center’s catalog identifies her as born in 1904.

Taught briefly before Atlanta’s restrictions on married women teachers ended her classroom career.
Founded Ebenezer Baptist Church’s choir and served as its organist and choir director for decades. She helped organize the church’s musical and women’s activities.
Participated in the NAACP, YWCA, and Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom.
Worked with Coretta Scott King and Christine King Farris to restore Martin Luther King Jr.’s birth home as a place the public could visit.
Was killed while playing the organ during Sunday worship at Ebenezer in June 1974.
Sources differ on her birth year: the Stanford King Institute gives 1903, while Atlanta History Center’s catalog identifies her as born in 1904.
